ad: Blue, yellow and red vertical stripes with the national coat of arms in the centre. The colours match those of neighbouring France and Spain, whose influence shaped Andorra's history. The arms show the cows of Béarn and the symbols of the Catalan and Urgell counts.
ae: A red vertical band at the hoist with green, white and black horizontal stripes. The four colours are the Pan-Arab colours, shared by many Arab nations and symbolising Arab unity. Green stands for fertility, white for neutrality and peace, black for strength, and red for unity.
af: Black, red and green vertical stripes with the national emblem in the centre. Black recalls the country's troubled past, red the blood shed for independence, and green hope and prosperity. The emblem shows a mosque with a mihrab, wheat ears and the Islamic declaration of faith.
ag: A red field with a downward black triangle holding a rising sun in yellow, blue and white. The sun symbolises a new era after independence, black the African heritage of the people, blue hope, and white the sand and sea. The red stands for the people's energy. The V shape represents victory.
ai: A British Blue Ensign with the Union Jack in the corner and the territory's coat of arms on the fly. The arms show three dolphins in a circle, symbolising endurance, unity and strength, above a turquoise wavy base representing the sea.
al: A red field with a black double-headed eagle in the centre. The eagle is the emblem of the 15th-century hero Skanderbeg, who fought the Ottomans. Red represents the bravery and blood of the people, and black stands for the eagle and for defiance of oppression.
am: Red, blue and orange horizontal stripes. Red represents the Armenian highland, the blood shed for survival and Christian faith. Blue stands for the sky and the will to live peacefully, and orange for the country's courage and hard-working people.
ao: A red stripe above a black one, with a yellow emblem in the centre made of a half cog wheel and a machete with a star. Red represents the blood shed in the fight against colonialism, and black stands for Africa. The cog and machete symbolise workers and farmers, and the star stands for progress and international solidarity.
aq: Antarctica has no official national flag, since no country owns it. An informal design widely used is the 'True South' flag, which shows a white silhouette of the continent on a blue background. Blue evokes the surrounding Southern Ocean and sky, and white the ice.
ar: Light blue, white and light blue horizontal stripes with a golden Sun of May in the centre. The colours come from the cockade used during the 1810 May Revolution, and the blue and white also evoke the sky and clouds. The sun, with a human face and 32 rays, represents Inti, the Inca sun god, and independence.
as: A white triangle bordered in red on a blue field, holding a bald eagle that clutches a Samoan war club and a fly whisk. The red, white and blue match the United States flag. The club and whisk are traditional symbols of Samoan chiefly authority.
at: Red, white and red horizontal stripes, one of the oldest national flags in the world. Legend says Duke Leopold V's white tunic was soaked in blood in the Siege of Acre in 1191, leaving only a white band where his belt had been. The colours come from the Babenberg dynasty's coat of arms.
au: A blue ensign with the Union Jack in the corner, the Commonwealth Star and the Southern Cross. The Union Jack recalls Australia's British origins and the star has seven points for the six states and the territories. The five stars of the Southern Cross are a constellation visible in the southern sky.
aw: A light blue field with two narrow yellow horizontal stripes near the bottom and a red four-pointed star with a white border at the top left. Blue represents the sea and sky, yellow the sun and gold, and the star the island itself. The four points stand for the four compass directions and the places Aruba's people came from.
ax: A blue field with a red Nordic cross edged in gold-yellow. The Nordic cross shows the islands' Scandinavian identity. The blue, yellow and red combine the colours of Sweden (blue and yellow) and Finland (red from its historic arms), reflecting the islands' Swedish-speaking culture within Finland.
az: Blue, red and green horizontal stripes with a white crescent and eight-pointed star on the red band. Blue stands for the Turkic heritage, red for modernisation and progress, and green for Islam. The crescent represents Islam and the star's eight points stand for the Turkic peoples.
ba: A blue field with a yellow right triangle and a diagonal line of white stars. The triangle represents the three constituent peoples, the Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs, and also the shape of the country. Blue and yellow with the white stars echo the flag of Europe, showing aspirations to join it.
bb: Three vertical bands of ultramarine, gold and ultramarine, with a black trident head on the gold band. The blue stands for the sea and sky and the gold for the sand. The broken trident, taken from the old colonial badge, symbolises breaking away from the colonial past, and its three points stand for the principles of democracy.
bd: A red disc on a dark green field. The green represents the lush land of Bangladesh and the red disc the rising sun and the blood of those who died in the 1971 independence struggle. The disc is slightly off-centre so it looks centred when flying.
be: Black, yellow and red vertical stripes. The colours come from the coat of arms of the Duchy of Brabant, a black lion on a gold field with a red tongue and claws, adopted during the 1830 revolution. They are often said to stand for the strength, wealth and bravery of the nation.
bf: Red over green horizontal stripes with a yellow five-pointed star in the centre. Red represents the revolution and green the country's agriculture and wealth. The star is the guiding light of the revolution. The flag was adopted in 1984 under Thomas Sankara and uses Pan-African colours.
bg: White, green and red horizontal stripes. White stands for peace and freedom, green for the country's agriculture and forests, and red for the courage of the people. It is based on Pan-Slavic colours and the flag of Russia, which helped free Bulgaria from the Ottomans.
bh: A white band at the hoist and a red field, separated by five white triangles forming a zigzag edge. Red is the traditional colour of Gulf Arab flags and the five points represent the five pillars of Islam. The design has been used since the 19th century.
bi: A white saltire dividing the flag into red and green triangles, with a white disc in the centre bearing three red stars outlined in green. The stars stand for the national motto of unity, work and progress. Red represents the struggle for independence, green hope, and white peace.
bj: A green vertical band at the hoist with yellow over red horizontal bands. The colours are the Pan-African colours: green for hope and the renewal of nature, yellow for the savanna and the wealth of the land, and red for the blood of ancestors and the courage of the people.
bl: Saint Barthélemy uses the French tricolour of blue, white and red vertical stripes as its official flag. The island also has an unofficial local flag with the coat of arms on a white field, showing a crown, a shield with fleurs-de-lis and pelicans for the island.
bm: A British Red Ensign with the Union Jack in the corner and the territory's coat of arms on the fly. The shield shows a red lion holding a shield with a wrecked ship, the Sea Venture, which was wrecked on Bermuda in 1609 and led to the island's settlement.
bn: A yellow field crossed by white and black diagonal stripes, with the national emblem in red in the centre. Yellow is the colour of the Sultan, while the white and black stripes represent the chief ministers. The emblem holds a crescent, a parasol, a flag and winged arms, symbolising Islam and the state's rulers and care of its people.
bo: Red, yellow and green horizontal stripes, with the national coat of arms on the yellow band. Red stands for the bravery of the army and blood shed in the fight for independence, yellow for the nation's mineral wealth, and green for the fertility of the land.
bq: The Caribbean Netherlands has no single flag, as it is made up of the islands Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. Each uses its own flag. Bonaire's has a blue, yellow and white design with a compass rose, while the Netherlands' red, white and blue tricolour is the national symbol.
br: A green field with a yellow rhombus holding a blue globe with a white banner reading 'Ordem e Progresso'. Green represents the forests and yellow the gold, or the House of Braganza and Habsburg. The globe has 27 stars in the pattern of the sky over Rio de Janeiro on the day the republic was proclaimed, one for each state.
bs: Aquamarine, gold and aquamarine horizontal stripes with a black triangle at the hoist. Aquamarine represents the surrounding sea, gold the sand and the sun, and black the strength and unity of the people.
bt: A flag split diagonally into yellow and orange-red halves, with a white dragon across the middle. The dragon, called Druk, is the thunder dragon of Bhutanese myth and gives the country its name, 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'. Yellow represents the king's secular authority and orange the Buddhist spiritual tradition. The white stands for purity and the jewels in its claws for wealth.
bv: Bouvet Island is an uninhabited Norwegian territory and uses the flag of Norway: a red field with a blue-bordered white Nordic cross. The red, white and blue colours recall France, the United Kingdom and the United States, which influenced Norway's democracy.
bw: A light blue field with a black horizontal band edged in white across the middle. Blue represents water, especially rain, which is vital in the dry country and also appears in the national motto 'Pula'. The black and white stripe stands for racial harmony between black and white citizens.
by: A red band above a green one with a white-and-red ornamental pattern on a vertical band at the hoist. The pattern is a traditional Belarusian embroidery design. Red is often said to stand for the past, battles and the sun, and green for forests, fields and hope.
bz: A blue field with red stripes at the top and bottom and a white disc in the middle holding the coat of arms. The arms are framed by a wreath of 50 leaves, marking 1950, when the independence movement began. They show two woodcutters, a tree and a ship, reflecting the logging history. Blue and red come from the colours of the country's two main political parties.
ca: A red field with a white square holding a red 11-pointed maple leaf. The maple leaf has been a Canadian emblem for centuries. Red and white are the national colours, taken from the cross of St George and later royal colours. The flag was adopted in 1965 and is often called the Maple Leaf.
cc: A green field with a gold palm tree on a gold island at the top left, a gold crescent at the top right and the Southern Cross constellation of five stars. Green and gold are Australia's national colours, as the territory belongs to Australia. The crescent represents Islam, the main religion of the Cocos Malay people.
cd: A sky blue field crossed by a diagonal red stripe edged in yellow, with a yellow star at the top left. The star symbolises a bright future, the blue stands for peace, the red for the blood of the country's martyrs, and the yellow for wealth. It has been used since 2006.
cf: Four horizontal bands of blue, white, green and yellow crossed by a vertical red stripe, with a yellow star in the top left. The red, blue, white and yellow-green mix the French tricolour with the Pan-African colours, standing for unity between Europe and Africa. The star represents a future hope.
cg: A diagonal tricolour of green, yellow and red from the hoist, using the Pan-African colours. Green stands for forests and agriculture, yellow for the people's friendship and nobility, and red for the blood shed in the struggle for independence.
ch: A red square flag with a white cross in the centre. It is one of only two square national flags, along with the Vatican. The cross is the symbol of Christianity and goes back to the medieval Swiss Confederacy's battle flags. Red and white have been the colours of the Swiss since the Middle Ages.
ci: Orange, white and green vertical stripes. Orange stands for the savanna in the north and the nation's land, white for peace and unity, and green for the forests in the south and for hope. It is the mirror image of Ireland's flag.
ck: A blue ensign with the Union Jack in the canton and a ring of 15 white stars on the fly. The stars represent the 15 islands of the Cook Islands. The blue stands for the Pacific Ocean and the nation's peaceful character.
cl: A white stripe on top of a red one, with a blue square holding a white star at the upper left. White stands for the snow of the Andes, red for the blood shed for independence, and blue for the sky and the Pacific Ocean. The star is a guide to progress and honour.
cm: Green, red and yellow vertical stripes with a yellow star in the centre of the red band. The colours are the Pan-African colours. Green represents the forests of the south, red unity, and yellow the sun and savannas of the north. The star is the star of unity.
cn: A red field with a large yellow star and four smaller yellow stars at the top left. Red represents the Communist revolution, and yellow the bright, golden land and the Chinese people. The large star represents the Communist Party and the four smaller ones stand for the social classes: workers, peasants, petty bourgeoisie and patriotic capitalists.
co: Yellow, blue and red horizontal stripes, with the yellow stripe twice as wide. Yellow stands for the gold, sovereignty and justice of the land, blue for the seas and rivers, and red for the blood shed for freedom. It follows the design of Francisco de Miranda's flag.
cr: Five horizontal stripes of blue, white, red, white and blue, with the red one wider. Blue stands for the sky, opportunities and perseverance, white for peace and wisdom, and red for the blood shed by the nation's people and for warmth and generosity. It was inspired by the French tricolour.
cu: Five horizontal blue and white stripes with a red triangle at the hoist holding a white star. The three blue stripes represent the three departments the island was divided into originally. The white stripes stand for the purity of the independence cause, the red triangle for the blood shed in the struggle, and the lone star for liberty.
cv: A blue field with a white-red-white horizontal band near the bottom and a circle of ten yellow stars. The ten stars represent the ten islands, blue stands for the ocean and sky, and the white and red stripes for the road to nation-building through peace and effort.
cw: A blue field with a yellow horizontal stripe below the middle and two white stars at the upper left. Blue represents the sea and sky, yellow the sun, and the two stars the two main islands, Curaçao and the smaller Klein Curaçao. The stars have five and six points.
cx: A flag split diagonally into blue and green, with a yellow disc in the centre holding a green map of the island. The Southern Cross appears on the blue half and a golden bosun bird, native to the island, on the green. Blue stands for the Indian Ocean and green for the island's rainforest. It is an Australian territory.
cy: A white field with a copper-coloured silhouette of the island above two crossed green olive branches. The copper colour recalls the island's name, from the Greek for copper. The olive branches symbolise peace between the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities. The flag deliberately avoids red and blue to remain neutral.
cz: White and red horizontal stripes with a blue triangle at the hoist. White and red are the traditional colours of Bohemia. The blue triangle comes from the Moravian and Slovak coats of arms, and was added when Czechoslovakia was formed to distinguish it from the flag of Poland.
de: Black, red and gold horizontal stripes. The colours date back to the 19th century liberal and nationalist movements and the 1848 revolution, and are associated with unity, freedom and democracy. They are said to derive from the uniforms of Lützow's volunteer corps against Napoleon.
dj: Light blue and green horizontal stripes with a white triangle at the hoist holding a red star. Blue stands for the sea and sky and for the Issa Somali people, green for the earth and the Afar people, and white for peace. The red star represents unity and the blood shed for independence.
dk: A red field with a white Scandinavian cross. Known as the Dannebrog, it is among the oldest national flags still in use. Legend says it fell from the sky during a battle in Estonia in 1219 and led the Danes to victory. The Nordic cross design was copied by other Scandinavian countries.
dm: A green field with a cross of yellow, black and white stripes, a red disc holding a Sisserou parrot and a ring of ten green stars. Green stands for the island's lush forests, and the cross for Christianity. Yellow stands for the indigenous people, citrus and sunshine, black for the African heritage and fertile soil, and white for water and clean rivers. The ten stars are the parishes.
do: A white cross dividing the flag into four rectangles, two blue and two red, with the coat of arms in the centre. Blue stands for liberty, red for the blood of heroes, and the white cross for the sacrifice and the unity of the people. The arms hold an open Bible, the only national flag to do so.
dz: A flag split vertically into green and white halves, with a red crescent and star in the middle. Green stands for Islam and nature, white for purity and peace, and red for the blood of martyrs in the fight for independence. The crescent and star are traditional Islamic symbols.
ec: Yellow, blue and red horizontal stripes with the national coat of arms in the centre, and the yellow stripe twice as wide. Yellow stands for the country's fertile land and gold, blue for the sky and ocean, and red for the blood shed for independence. The arms show Mount Chimborazo, the Guayas River and a steamship.
ee: Blue, black and white horizontal stripes. Blue stands for the sky, lakes and sea and for loyalty, black for the soil of the homeland and the past suffering of the people, and white for the snow, the striving for enlightenment and purity.
eg: Red, white and black horizontal stripes with the golden Eagle of Saladin in the middle. The colours are the Pan-Arab colours: red for the struggle against the monarchy and the blood of martyrs, white for the bright future and the revolution's peaceful nature, and black for the end of oppression.
eh: Black, white and green horizontal stripes with a red triangle at the hoist and a red crescent and star on the white band. It uses the Pan-Arab colours. The crescent and star are symbols of Islam. The flag is used by the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, which claims the territory.
er: A red triangle pointing from the hoist, flanked by green above and blue below, with a gold olive wreath and branch in the red triangle. Green stands for agriculture, blue for the Red Sea and marine resources, and red for the blood shed for independence. The olive wreath is a symbol of peace.
es: Red, yellow and red horizontal stripes, the yellow band being twice as wide, with the coat of arms on the yellow band. The red and yellow come from the historic Aragonese crown. The arms contain the pillars of Hercules and the symbols of the old kingdoms, including Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre.
et: Green, yellow and red horizontal stripes with a blue disc holding a yellow pentagram star with rays. These were the first of the Pan-African colours, inspiring many other African flags. Green stands for the land and hope, yellow for peace and natural wealth, and red for strength. The star stands for the unity and equality of the nation's peoples.
fi: A white field with a blue Nordic cross. The white represents the country's snow and the blue the thousands of lakes and the sky. The cross design shows Finland's Christian heritage and its place in the Nordic family of countries.
fj: A light blue field with the British Union Jack in the canton and the national shield on the fly. Light blue represents the Pacific Ocean and the Union Jack the country's colonial history. The shield holds a lion with a cocoa pod, sugar cane, coconut palm, bananas and a dove of peace.
fk: A blue ensign with the Union Jack and the territory's coat of arms on the fly. The arms show a ram on grass above a ship, the Desire, named after John Davis's ship, and the motto 'Desire the Right'. The ram stands for sheep farming, the island's main industry.
fm: A light blue field with four white stars arranged in a diamond. The blue represents the Pacific Ocean, and the four stars stand for the four states: Chuuk, Kosrae, Pohnpei and Yap. The stars were originally six, representing the Trust Territory's districts.
fo: A white field with a red cross edged in blue. The Nordic cross shows ties to Scandinavia and the colours are those of the Faroese, Norway and Iceland. Blue and white represent the sea and sky and red the heritage of the islanders. It is known as Merkið, 'the banner'.
fr: Blue, white and red vertical stripes. Blue and red are the colours of Paris and white was the colour of the royal house of Bourbon. The tricolour became a symbol of the French Revolution, and its ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity, and has inspired many other national flags.
ga: Green, yellow and blue horizontal stripes. Green stands for the country's vast forests, yellow for the equator, which passes through Gabon, and the sun, and blue for the Atlantic Ocean to the west.
gb: The Union Jack combines the crosses of three patron saints: the red cross of St George of England, the white saltire of St Andrew of Scotland and the red saltire of St Patrick of Ireland. It represents the union of the kingdoms. Wales is not separately shown, as it was already part of England when the flag was designed.
gd: A red border with six yellow stars, around yellow and green triangles, with a nutmeg and a gold star on the left. The nutmeg stands for the island's spice industry. Red stands for unity and courage, yellow for the sun and wisdom, and green for vegetation and agriculture. The seven stars are the parishes.
ge: A white field with a large red cross and four smaller red crosses in each quarter. This is the Five Cross Flag, linked to the Crusades and the medieval Kingdom of Georgia. The red cross is St George's cross, symbolising the nation's Christian faith, and the white stands for peace and purity.
gf: French Guiana uses the French tricolour of blue, white and red vertical stripes as its official flag. It is an overseas department of France. A green and yellow local flag with a red star is also used by some residents.
gg: A white field with a red St George's cross and a gold cross inside it. The gold cross was added in 1985 and recalls William the Conqueror's cross on his banner, Guernsey's link to the Duchy of Normandy. The red and white of the cross shows its English connection.
gh: Red, gold and green horizontal stripes with a black star in the centre. These are Pan-African colours, with red for the blood shed for independence, gold for the mineral wealth, and green for forests and natural riches. The black star is the 'lodestar of African freedom'.
gi: A white band above a red band, with a red castle with three towers and a golden key hanging from the gate. The castle and key come from the arms granted in 1502 by Queen Isabella of Castile and represent Gibraltar as the key to the Mediterranean.
gl: White and red horizontal halves with a counter-changed red and white disc. The white stands for the ice and snow, and the red for the ocean. The disc stands for the sun, with its lower half in red like the sun's reflection on the sea, and its upper half in white like the ice.
gm: Red, blue and green horizontal stripes separated by thin white stripes. Red stands for the sun and the central savanna, blue for the Gambia River, which runs through the country, and green for the forests and agriculture. The white stripes stand for peace and unity.
gn: Red, yellow and green vertical stripes using the Pan-African colours. Red stands for the people's sacrifice and work, yellow for the sun and the nation's wealth, and green for the vegetation and agriculture. The motto is 'work, justice, solidarity'.
gp: Guadeloupe uses the French tricolour of blue, white and red vertical stripes as its official flag. The island also has an unofficial local flag, with a sun and a green field, used by independence movements.
gq: Green, white and red horizontal stripes with a blue triangle at the hoist and the national coat of arms in the centre. Green stands for the country's natural resources, white for peace, red for the blood shed for independence, and blue for the sea linking the mainland to the islands. The arms show a silk-cotton tree and six stars for the mainland and islands.
gr: Nine blue and white horizontal stripes, with a white cross on a blue square at the upper left. The nine stripes are said to stand for the syllables of the Greek motto 'Freedom or Death', or for the nine Muses. Blue represents the sea and sky, white the purity of the struggle for independence, and the cross the Greek Orthodox faith.
gs: A British Blue Ensign with the Union Jack in the corner and the territory's coat of arms on the fly. The arms show a Scottish lion, a fur seal and a reindeer, which stand for the wildlife of these remote islands. Its motto is 'Leo Terram Propriam Protegat', meaning 'let the lion protect its own land'.
gt: Light blue, white and light blue vertical stripes with the coat of arms in the centre. Blue stands for the Pacific and Caribbean oceans and the sky, and white for peace and purity. The arms hold a quetzal, the national bird, a scroll with the date of independence, and crossed rifles and swords.
gu: A dark blue field with a thin red border and a central oval holding a coconut tree and a proa, an outrigger canoe, on a beach. The red and blue are the colours of the United States. The scene shows a view from the island's Agana Bay and the territory's name in red letters.
gw: A red vertical band with a black star at the hoist, and yellow over green horizontal stripes. The Pan-African colours: red for the blood shed in the independence struggle, yellow for the sun and wealth, and green for hope and nature. The black star stands for African unity.
gy: A green field with a gold arrowhead outlined in white and a red triangle edged in black. Known as the Golden Arrowhead, the green stands for forests and agriculture, white for rivers and water, gold for mineral wealth, red for the zeal and sacrifice of nation-building, and black for endurance.
hk: A red field with a white five-petalled bauhinia flower, each petal carrying a red star. The bauhinia is the emblem of the territory, and the red stars recall the Chinese flag. Red stands for the motherland and the white flower for Hong Kong, reflecting 'one country, two systems'.
hm: Heard Island and McDonald Islands are an uninhabited Australian territory and use the flag of Australia: a blue ensign with the Union Jack, the Commonwealth Star and the Southern Cross constellation.
hn: Blue, white and blue horizontal stripes with five blue stars in the centre. Blue stands for the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea and the sky, and white for peace and prosperity. The five stars represent the five countries of the former Federal Republic of Central America.
hr: Red, white and blue horizontal stripes with the coat of arms in the centre. The colours are the Pan-Slavic colours. The arms hold a red and white chequerboard shield, the šahovnica, topped by a crown made of five smaller shields representing historic regions of Croatia.
ht: Blue over red horizontal bands with a white rectangle holding the coat of arms. It originated when Jean-Jacques Dessalines removed the white band from the French tricolour in 1803. Blue stands for the Black population and red for the mixed-race people. The arms feature a palm tree topped by a liberty cap and cannons, and the motto 'Unity makes strength'.
hu: Red, white and green horizontal stripes. The colours date from the Hungarian coat of arms and were used in the 1848 revolution. Red is said to stand for strength, white for faithfulness, and green for hope. They are also said to stand for blood, freedom and the land.
id: Red over white horizontal stripes. Red stands for courage and the human body, and white for purity and the human soul. The colours date back to the 13th-century Majapahit Empire. It is almost identical to Monaco's flag, differing only in proportions.
ie: Green, white and orange vertical stripes. Green represents the Gaelic and Catholic tradition, orange the followers of William of Orange, who are largely Protestant, and white a lasting peace between them. It was first presented in 1848 as a symbol of unity.
il: A white field with a blue Star of David between two blue horizontal stripes. The design is based on the Jewish prayer shawl, the tallit, which is white with blue stripes. The Star of David is a symbol of Judaism and Jewish identity. The flag was adopted in 1948.
im: A red field with the triskelion, three armoured legs radiating from the centre. The triskelion is an ancient symbol of the island, and the legs run in a pattern that suggests they continue in motion. The island's Latin motto means 'Whichever way you throw me, I will stand'.
in: Saffron, white and green horizontal stripes with a navy blue 24-spoke wheel, the Ashoka Chakra, in the centre. Saffron stands for courage and sacrifice, white for peace and truth, and green for faith and fertility. The wheel represents the law of dharma and the continuous progress of the nation.
io: A white field with blue wavy stripes, the Union Jack in the canton and a palm tree beneath a gold crown. The waves represent the Indian Ocean and the palm tree the islands. The Union Jack shows its status as a British overseas territory.
iq: Red, white and black horizontal stripes with the green words 'Allahu Akbar' in Arabic script across the white band. The colours are the Pan-Arab colours. The writing, meaning 'God is the greatest', was added in 1991. The flag has changed several times since 2004.
ir: Green, white and red horizontal stripes with the national emblem in red in the centre and the words 'Allahu Akbar' repeated along the edges of the green and red bands. Green stands for Islam and growth, white for peace, and red for bravery and martyrdom. The emblem is a stylised form of the word 'Allah'.
is: A blue field with a white-bordered red Nordic cross. Blue stands for the mountains and Atlantic Ocean, white for the ice and snow, and red for the volcanic fires of the island. The cross shows the country's Nordic heritage.
it: Green, white and red vertical stripes, based on the French tricolour and adopted during the Napoleonic era. Green was the colour of the uniform of the Milanese Civic Guard, and white and red were the colours of Milan. Later they were said to represent hope, faith and charity. Green also stands for the plains, white for the Alps and red for the blood of unification.
je: A white field with a red saltire, with the badge of Jersey on the top. The saltire is the cross of St Patrick and the crown shows the link to the monarchy. The shield shows three leopards, the arms of the Duke of Normandy, who ruled the island in the Middle Ages.
jm: A gold diagonal cross dividing the flag into green triangles at the top and bottom and black at the hoist and fly. The flag was designed to be unlike any other. Black stands for the hardships overcome, gold for the sunshine and natural wealth, and green for hope and agricultural resources.
jo: Black, white and green horizontal stripes with a red triangle at the hoist holding a white seven-pointed star. The colours are the Pan-Arab colours, standing for the Abbasid, Umayyad and Fatimid caliphates, and the red triangle for the Hashemite dynasty and the Arab Revolt. The seven points stand for the seven verses of the opening chapter of the Quran.
jp: A white field with a red disc in the centre. Known as the Hinomaru, 'circle of the sun', it symbolises the sun and Japan's name, 'Land of the Rising Sun'. White represents honesty and purity, and the red disc sincerity, brightness and warmth.
ke: Black, red and green horizontal stripes separated by white fringes, with a traditional Maasai shield and two crossed spears in the centre. Black stands for the people, red for the blood shed in the struggle for independence, green for the land and natural wealth, and white for peace. The shield and spears symbolise the defence of freedom.
kg: A red field with a yellow sun at the centre with forty rays, around a tündük, the crown of a yurt. Red stands for bravery and the national hero Manas. The forty rays represent the forty tribes united by Manas, and the tündük the home and the universe.
kh: Blue, red and blue horizontal stripes with the white outline of Angkor Wat in the centre. It is one of only a few national flags to show a building. Blue stands for the monarchy's royal power, red for the nation, and white for religion. Angkor Wat is the most famous symbol of Khmer civilisation.
ki: A red field with a golden frigatebird flying above a rising sun, and three wavy bands of white and blue at the base. The wavy stripes show the Pacific Ocean and the three island groups, the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line Islands. The frigate bird stands for power and freedom, and the rising sun for the equatorial location.
km: Four horizontal stripes of yellow, white, red and blue with a green triangle at the hoist holding a white crescent and four stars. The four stripes and stars represent the four islands, Grande Comore, Anjouan, Mohéli and Mayotte. Green and the crescent represent Islam, the main religion.
kn: A diagonal green and red field separated by a black band edged in yellow, with two white stars. Green stands for the fertile land, red for the struggle against slavery and colonialism, yellow for sunshine, and black for the African heritage. The two white stars represent hope and liberty, and the two islands.
kp: A red central band with a white disc holding a red star, between thin white stripes and larger blue stripes at the top and bottom. Red stands for revolutionary traditions and patriotism, blue for sovereignty, peace and friendship, and white for purity. The red star symbolises the country's socialism.
kr: A white field with a central red and blue taegeuk circle, surrounded by four black trigrams in each corner. White stands for peace and purity. The taegeuk represents the balance of yin and yang, the harmony of opposites, and the trigrams stand for heaven, earth, fire and water.
kw: Green, white and red horizontal stripes with a black trapezoid at the hoist. The Pan-Arab colours: green stands for fertile lands, white for purity and honour, red for the blood on the swords of the Kuwaiti people, and black for the battlefields and the defeat of enemies.
ky: A British Blue Ensign with the Union Jack and the coat of arms of the islands on the fly. The shield shows three stars for the three islands, wavy blue and white lines for the sea, and a lion for Britain. The crest has a turtle and a pineapple, and the motto means 'He hath founded it upon the seas'.
kz: A sky blue field with a golden sun with 32 rays above a soaring steppe eagle, and a vertical ornamental pattern at the hoist. Sky blue stands for the endless sky and the Turkic peoples and the unity of the nation. The sun stands for life and energy, and the eagle for freedom and the spirit of the nation.
la: Red, blue and red horizontal stripes with a white disc in the centre. Red stands for the blood shed for independence, and blue for the Mekong River and the prosperity of the country. The white disc represents the moon over the river or the unity of the people under the government.
lb: Red, white and red horizontal stripes with a green cedar tree on the white band. The cedar is the national emblem, an ancient symbol of holiness, eternity and peace mentioned in the Bible. Red stands for sacrifice and the blood shed for independence, and white for peace and snow-capped mountains.
lc: A light blue field with a white-edged black and gold triangle in the centre. Blue stands for the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, gold for sunshine and prosperity, and black and white for the racial harmony between the African and European peoples. The triangles represent the island's volcanic Pitons.
li: Blue and red horizontal stripes with a golden crown in the upper hoist corner. Blue stands for the sky and red for the warmth of the hearth fires. The crown, added in 1937, symbolises the unity of people and the prince. It was added to distinguish the flag from Haiti's, which looks the same.
lk: A gold lion holding a sword on a maroon field, with green and orange vertical stripes at the hoist, all within a yellow border. The lion stands for the Sinhalese people and the sword for sovereignty. The green and orange stripes represent the Muslim and Tamil minorities, and the four leaves of the bo tree in the corners stand for Buddhist values.
lr: Eleven red and white horizontal stripes with a blue square holding a white star in the canton. It is modelled on the flag of the United States, with which Liberia has historical ties through freed American slaves. The eleven stripes stand for the eleven signers of the Declaration of Independence, and the star for the first independent African republic.
ls: Blue, white and green horizontal stripes with a black Basotho hat, the mokorotlo, in the centre. Blue stands for rain, white for peace, and green for prosperity. The hat is a traditional symbol of the Basotho people and the national emblem.
lt: Yellow, green and red horizontal stripes. Yellow stands for the sun, light and prosperity, green for the country's forests and nature and for hope, and red for the blood shed in defence of the homeland and the courage of the people.
lu: Red, white and light blue horizontal stripes. The colours come from the red lion arms of the Grand Duchy. It is very similar to the flag of the Netherlands, but with a lighter shade of blue and longer proportions.
lv: Carmine red and white horizontal stripes, with the white stripe being half the width of the red ones. According to legend, a Latvian chieftain was wounded in battle and wrapped in a white sheet, with only the edges stained with his blood. The dark red is a symbol of the willingness to sacrifice for freedom.
ly: Red, black and green horizontal stripes, with the black band twice as wide and a white crescent and star in the middle. Red stands for the blood shed during the fight against Italian rule, black for the dark days of colonisation, and green for Fezzan and the land. The crescent and star are symbols of Islam.
ma: A red field with a green pentagram, a five-pointed star known as Solomon's seal, in the centre. Red is the traditional colour of the Moroccan Alaouite dynasty, and also stands for bravery. The green star stands for Islam, the five pillars of Islam, wisdom, peace and health.
mc: Red over white horizontal stripes. The colours are taken from the arms of the House of Grimaldi, the ruling family. It is nearly identical to Indonesia's flag, but longer in proportion.
md: Blue, yellow and red vertical stripes with the coat of arms in the centre. The colours are the same as those of Romania, reflecting the shared language and history. The arms hold an aurochs head, the symbol of Moldavia, with a star, a rose and a crescent.
me: A red field with a gold border and the double-headed eagle in the centre. The eagle holds a sceptre and orb, and a lion on a shield on its chest. The red and gold are the colours of the old Petrović-Njegoš dynasty. The eagle symbolises sovereignty.
mf: The Collectivity of Saint Martin uses the French tricolour of blue, white and red vertical stripes as its official flag. The island is shared with Dutch Sint Maarten, and is a French overseas collectivity.
mg: A white vertical band at the hoist with red and green horizontal stripes. White stands for purity, red for sovereignty, and green for hope and the Hova people, with the colours also recalling the Merina kingdom. The flag shares the colours of the older kingdom's flags.
mh: A blue field with two diagonal orange and white bands rising from the lower hoist, and a white 24-pointed star at the upper left. Blue stands for the Pacific Ocean, orange for bravery, and white for peace. The star's 24 points stand for the municipalities, and the four longer rays for the Christian cross.
mk: A red field with a yellow sun at the centre whose eight rays extend to the edges of the flag. The design is a new sun on a new day of freedom. Red and yellow are the traditional colours of the country. The previous flag showed the Vergina Sun and was changed after a dispute with Greece.
ml: Green, yellow and red vertical stripes using the Pan-African colours. Green stands for the fertility of the land, yellow for the country's mineral wealth and purity, and red for the blood shed for independence. The flag is similar to those of several other African countries.
mm: Yellow, green and red horizontal stripes with a large white five-pointed star in the centre. Yellow stands for solidarity, green for peace, tranquillity and the lush environment, and red for courage and decisiveness. The white star stands for the union of the country.
mn: Red, blue and red vertical stripes with a yellow Soyombo symbol at the hoist. Red stands for progress and prosperity, and blue for the eternal blue sky. The Soyombo is a Buddhist symbol of independence and sovereignty, made of fire, sun, moon, and other elements.
mo: A green field with a white lotus flower above a bridge and water, below five gold stars. The lotus is the symbol of Macau, the bridge and water recall the city's geography. The five stars come from the Chinese flag. Green stands for peace.
mp: A blue field with a white star on a grey latte stone, circled by a wreath of flowers. The latte stone is a pillar used in the ancient Chamorro houses. The wreath is a traditional Pacific mwarmwar, a lei, and the blue stands for the Pacific Ocean.
mq: Martinique's official flag is the French tricolour of blue, white and red vertical stripes. A regional flag with a blue background, white cross and snakes also exists but is used unofficially.
mr: A green field with a gold crescent and star between red stripes at the top and bottom. Green and the crescent and star represent Islam, the country's main religion. Gold stands for the Sahara desert, and the red stripes added in 2017 for the blood shed for independence.
ms: A British Blue Ensign with the Union Jack and the territory's coat of arms on the fly. The arms show a woman with a cross and a harp, representing the Irish heritage of the island, which is sometimes called the 'Emerald Isle of the Caribbean'.
mt: White and red vertical stripes with a George Cross edged in red in the upper hoist corner. The colours are taken from the Arab Count Roger of Sicily's banner. The George Cross was awarded by King George VI in 1942 for the island's bravery during the Second World War.
mu: Four horizontal stripes of red, blue, yellow and green. Red stands for the struggle for independence, blue for the Indian Ocean, yellow for the golden light of independence, and green for the island's vegetation and agriculture.
mv: A red field with a green rectangle holding a white crescent. Red stands for the blood shed by national heroes in defence of the country, green for life, progress and prosperity, and the white crescent for Islam, the country's religion.
mw: Black, red and green horizontal stripes with a red rising sun with rays on the black stripe. Black stands for the African people, red for the blood of the struggle for freedom, and green for the nature and ever-green land. The rising sun symbolises the dawn of hope and freedom.
mx: Green, white and red vertical stripes with the coat of arms in the centre. Green stands for hope, white for unity and religion, and red for the blood of the national heroes. The arms show an eagle on a prickly pear cactus devouring a snake, from the Aztec legend of the founding of Tenochtitlan.
my: Fourteen red and white horizontal stripes with a blue canton holding a yellow crescent and a 14-pointed star. The stripes and star points represent the 13 states and the federal territories. Blue stands for unity, red for bravery, and yellow is the colour of the royal rulers. The crescent stands for Islam.
mz: Green, black and yellow horizontal stripes separated by white fringes, with a red triangle at the hoist holding a yellow star, an open book and a crossed AK-47 and hoe. Green stands for the land, black for Africa, yellow for minerals, white for peace, and red for the struggle for independence. The rifle and hoe stand for defence and agriculture, and the book for education.
na: A diagonal red stripe edged in white, with a blue triangle at the upper hoist holding a golden sun with 12 rays, and a green triangle at the lower fly. Blue stands for the sky and the Atlantic Ocean, red for the people and their heroism, green for vegetation, white for peace and unity, and the sun for life and energy.
nc: A flag with horizontal stripes of blue, red and green with a yellow disc holding the black symbol of a flèche faîtière, the pointed roof ornament of a Kanak chief's hut. It is flown alongside the French tricolour. Blue stands for the sky and ocean, red for the Kanak people's struggle, green for the land, and yellow for the sun.
ne: Orange, white and green horizontal stripes with an orange disc in the centre of the white stripe. Orange stands for the Sahara Desert in the north, white for purity and the Niger River, and green for the fertile land and hope in the south. The disc represents the sun.
nf: Green, white and green vertical stripes with a green Norfolk Island pine in the centre of the white stripe. The Norfolk Island pine is the island's symbol and native tree. Green stands for the island's vegetation and white for peace. It is a territory of Australia.
ng: Green, white and green vertical stripes. Green stands for the country's agriculture and natural wealth, and white for peace and unity. It was designed by Michael Taiwo Akinkunmi in 1959 and chosen in a national competition.
ni: Blue, white and blue horizontal stripes with the national coat of arms in the centre of the white band. Blue stands for the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, and white for the land between them. The arms show a triangle with five volcanoes and a rainbow and Phrygian cap, representing the former Central American union.
nl: Red, white and blue horizontal stripes. It descends from the Dutch revolt against Spain, and the orange-white-blue flag of William of Orange, with the orange turning red over time. It is the oldest tricolour in continuous use.
no: A red field with a blue-bordered white Nordic cross. It combines the Danish design with the colours of the French, British and American flags. Red, white and blue stand for liberty and democracy, which had inspired the Norwegians.
np: Two stacked red pennants with blue borders, holding a white moon and sun. It is the only non-rectangular national flag. The pennants represent the Himalayan mountains and the two religions, Hinduism and Buddhism. Red stands for the national flower, the rhododendron, and bravery, blue for peace, and the moon and sun for the nation's lasting endurance.
nr: A dark blue field with a thin gold horizontal stripe and a white twelve-pointed star below. The star represents the twelve original tribes of Nauru, and its position on the island's latitude, just south of the equator, shown by the gold line. Blue stands for the Pacific Ocean.
nu: A yellow field with the Union Jack in the canton and a blue disc holding a yellow star, with four smaller yellow stars. Yellow stands for the bright sun and the warmth of the Niuean people towards New Zealand. The Union Jack shows the link to the United Kingdom, and the blue disc and stars the Southern Cross.
nz: A blue ensign with the Union Jack in the canton and four red stars with white borders. The stars show the Southern Cross constellation, used by navigators in the southern hemisphere. The Union Jack recalls New Zealand's British colonial history.
om: A white, red and green horizontal stripes with a red vertical band at the hoist holding the national emblem, a khanjar dagger and crossed swords, in white. White stands for peace and prosperity, red for the battles against foreign invaders, and green for the fertility of the land and the Jebel Akhdar mountains.
pa: A flag divided into four quarters: white with a blue star at the top left, red at the top right, blue at the bottom left, and white with a red star at the bottom right. Blue and red stand for the two main political parties, the Conservatives and Liberals, and white for peace between them. The blue star stands for honesty and the red star for authority and law.
pe: Red, white and red vertical stripes. Legend says that General José de San Martín saw a flock of red and white flamingos while landing in Peru, which inspired the colours. Red stands for blood shed for independence and white for peace. The state flag has the coat of arms in the middle.
pf: Red, white and red horizontal stripes with a white band holding a blue wavy-lined disc with a golden sun and a traditional Polynesian outrigger canoe. The ship stands for the Polynesian people, the sun for the dawn, the blue wavy lines for the Pacific Ocean, and the white for peace.
pg: A diagonal split flag with red at the upper right holding a yellow bird of paradise, and black at the lower left holding the Southern Cross in white stars. The bird of paradise is the national bird, and black and red are traditional colours of the island's art. The Southern Cross is the constellation seen in the southern sky.
ph: A white equilateral triangle at the hoist with a blue stripe above a red one. The triangle stands for equality, with a golden sun of eight rays standing for the first provinces that rebelled against Spain, and three stars for the three main island groups: Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao. Blue stands for peace and truth, and red for patriotism and valour. The flag is flown upside down in wartime, with red on top.
pk: A dark green field with a white vertical band at the hoist and a white crescent and star in the centre. Green stands for the Muslim majority, and the white band for religious minorities. The crescent stands for progress and the star for light and knowledge.
pl: White over red horizontal stripes. The colours come from the coat of arms of Poland, a white eagle on a red field. White is often said to stand for peace and honesty, and red for the blood shed in the nation's struggle for independence and for courage.
pm: Saint Pierre and Miquelon use the French tricolour as their official flag. A local unofficial flag shows a sailing ship, the Grand Hermine, with three bands showing the Basque, Breton and Norman regions that settled the islands.
pn: A blue ensign with the Union Jack and the coat of arms on the fly. The arms show a shield with a ship's anchor and a Bible, with the wheelbarrow and the HMS Bounty's rudder, and a green and blue background, all referencing the Bounty mutineers who settled the island.
pr: Five red and white horizontal stripes with a blue triangle at the hoist holding a white star. It is modelled on the Cuban flag, from the shared fight against Spain, with the colours reversed. Red stands for the blood of the people, white for peace and liberty, and blue for the sky and sea.
ps: Black, white and green horizontal stripes with a red triangle at the hoist. These are the Pan-Arab colours: black for the Abbasid Caliphate, white for the Umayyad Caliphate, green for the Fatimid Caliphate, and red for the Hashemite dynasty and the Arab Revolt. The flag was adopted in 1964 and is a symbol of Palestinian identity.
pt: A green vertical band at the hoist and a larger red band, with the national coat of arms where they meet. Green stands for hope, red for the blood of those who died for Portugal, and the arms show a shield with five blue shields for the Portuguese kings, on an armillary sphere recalling the Age of Discovery.
pw: A light blue field with a golden-yellow disc placed slightly towards the hoist. Blue stands for the Pacific Ocean, and the disc for the full moon, a symbol of peace, love and tranquillity and the traditional time for fishing and celebrations. The disc is off-centre so that it looks centred when the flag flutters.
py: Red, white and blue horizontal stripes with the national emblem on the front and the treasury seal on the back. It is the only national flag with a different design on each side. Red stands for justice and equality, white for peace, and blue for liberty. The front shows a star surrounded by a palm and olive branch.
qa: A maroon field with a white serrated band at the hoist, with nine white points. The maroon colour comes from the dye used by Qatari fishermen, which darkened under the sun. The nine points stand for Qatar's status as the ninth member of the 'reconciled emirates' of the Persian Gulf region.
re: Réunion uses the French tricolour of blue, white and red vertical stripes as its official flag. It is an overseas department of France. Several unofficial local flags also exist.
ro: Blue, yellow and red vertical stripes. Blue stands for liberty, yellow for justice, and red for brotherhood. The colours first appeared in the 1848 revolution and are the same as Andorra's and Chad's flags. The yellow stripe is also said to represent the country's mineral wealth.
rs: Red, blue and white horizontal stripes with the coat of arms on the left. These are the Pan-Slavic colours. The arms show a double-headed white eagle and a red shield with a cross and four Cyrillic letters 'S', which stand for 'Only unity saves the Serbs'.
ru: White, blue and red horizontal stripes. The colours are the Pan-Slavic colours, and they were first used by Peter the Great. White is often said to stand for nobility and frankness, blue for faithfulness and honesty, and red for courage and love.
rw: Blue, yellow and green horizontal stripes with a golden sun with 24 rays in the upper fly. Blue stands for happiness and peace, yellow for economic development, and green for hope of prosperity. The sun stands for enlightenment, and it was adopted in 2001 to leave behind the 1994 genocide.
sa: A green field with the Arabic Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, in white above a sword. It reads: 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the Messenger of God.' Green is the colour of Islam, and the sword represents justice and the founding of the kingdom. The flag is never flown at half-mast because it carries the Shahada.
sb: A diagonal split flag in blue and green with a yellow stripe and five white stars in the blue triangle. Blue stands for the ocean and green for the land, yellow for the sun, and the five stars for the five original districts of the islands.
sc: Five diagonal bands fanning out from the lower hoist in blue, yellow, red, white and green. Blue stands for the sky and sea, yellow for the sun, red for the people's determination, white for social justice and harmony, and green for the land and natural environment. It was adopted in 1996.
sd: Red, white and black horizontal stripes with a green triangle at the hoist. The Pan-Arab colours: red stands for the struggle, white for peace, optimism and light, and black for the Sudan and the Mahdist revolution. Green stands for Islam, prosperity and agriculture.
se: A blue field with a yellow Nordic cross. The colours come from the national coat of arms, with three golden crowns on a blue field. Legend traces the flag back to a 12th-century crusade of King Eric IX. The cross shows Sweden's Christian heritage.
sg: Red over white horizontal stripes with a white crescent and five white stars in a circle at the upper hoist. Red stands for universal brotherhood and equality, and white for pure and lasting virtue. The crescent represents a young, rising nation, and the five stars its ideals: democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality.
sh: A British Blue Ensign with the Union Jack and the territory's coat of arms on the fly. The arms show a rocky coastal scene with a ship, with a wirebird, the island's endemic bird, and a Saint Helena plover on a shield.
si: White, blue and red horizontal stripes with the coat of arms at the upper hoist. These are Pan-Slavic colours. The arms show Mount Triglav, the highest peak, in white above wavy blue lines representing the sea and rivers, and three golden stars from the Counts of Celje.
sj: Svalbard and Jan Mayen are Norwegian territories and use the flag of Norway: a red field with a blue-bordered white Nordic cross. The red, white and blue stand for liberty and democracy.
sk: White, blue and red horizontal stripes with the national coat of arms at the hoist. These are the Pan-Slavic colours. The arms show a white double cross on a blue three-peaked mountain, representing the Tatra, Fatra and Matra mountains and the Christianity brought by Saints Cyril and Methodius.
sl: Green, white and blue horizontal stripes. Green stands for agriculture, natural resources and the mountains, white for unity and justice, and blue for the Atlantic Ocean and the natural harbour of Freetown, the capital.
sm: White and light blue horizontal stripes with the coat of arms in the centre. White stands for peace and the snow on Mount Titano, and light blue for the sky. The arms show three towers on three peaks of the mountain, and the motto 'Libertas', meaning freedom.
sn: Green, yellow and red vertical stripes with a green star in the centre. These are the Pan-African colours, with green for Islam and hope, yellow for natural wealth and progress, and red for life and sacrifice. The five-pointed star stands for unity and the nation's spirit.
so: A light blue field with a white five-pointed star in the centre. The blue was inspired by the United Nations flag, in recognition of its help to the country's independence. The five points of the star stand for the five regions inhabited by Somalis: British Somaliland, Italian Somaliland, French Somaliland, Ogaden and northern Kenya.
sr: Five horizontal stripes: green, white, red, white and green, with a large yellow star in the centre of the wide red stripe. Green stands for fertility and hope, white for justice and freedom, and red for progress and love. The golden star stands for unity and a golden future.
ss: Black, red and green horizontal stripes separated by white fringes, with a blue triangle at the hoist holding a yellow star. Black stands for the people, red for the blood shed for freedom, green for the land, white for peace, and blue for the Nile. The yellow star stands for unity of the states.
st: Green, yellow and green horizontal stripes with a red triangle at the hoist and two black stars on the yellow band. The Pan-African colours: green stands for the country's vegetation, yellow for cocoa, and red for the struggle for independence. The two black stars stand for the two main islands.
sv: Blue, white and blue horizontal stripes with the coat of arms on the white band. The blue stands for the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, and the white for peace. The arms show a triangle with five volcanoes, a rainbow, and a Phrygian cap, as well as the motto 'God, Union, Liberty'.
sx: Red and blue horizontal stripes with a white triangle at the hoist holding the coat of arms. Red, white and blue are the Dutch colours, linked to the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The arms show the courthouse in Philipsburg, a sea and a yellow sun and flower.
sy: Red, white and black horizontal stripes with two green stars on the white band. They are the Pan-Arab colours. Red stands for the struggle and the blood shed for freedom, white for purity and a bright future, and black for the oppressed past. The two green stars recall Syria's union with Egypt.
sz: Blue, yellow, red, yellow and blue horizontal stripes with a Swazi shield and two spears and a staff in the centre. Blue stands for peace, red for past battles, and yellow for the country's resources. The black and white shield is made of cowhide, and stands for peaceful coexistence between black and white people.
tc: A British Blue Ensign with the Union Jack and the coat of arms on the fly. The arms show a conch shell, a spiny lobster and a Turks Head cactus, which are native to the islands and the source of their economy and name.
td: Blue, yellow and red vertical stripes. Blue stands for the sky, water and the south of the country, yellow for the sun and the desert in the north, and red for progress, unity and the sacrifice of the people. It is almost identical to the flag of Romania.
tf: A blue field with the French tricolour in the upper left corner and, on the right, a white emblem with stars and the letters TAAF. The stars include the Southern Cross, recalling the remote southern location, and the blue stands for the Southern Ocean. The territory has no permanent population.
tg: Five green and yellow horizontal stripes with a red square at the canton holding a white star. Green stands for hope and agriculture, yellow for the mines and the faith in work, and red for charity and the blood shed for independence. The white star stands for national independence.
th: Five horizontal stripes of red, white, blue, white and red, with the blue stripe being twice as wide. Red stands for the nation and the blood of life, white for religion and purity, and blue for the monarchy. It is known as the Trairanga, the tricolour.
tj: Red, white and green horizontal stripes with a golden crown and seven stars in an arc on the white band. Red stands for unity and the victory, white for purity and cotton, and green for nature and agriculture. The crown and seven stars stand for the nation and its people, and the number seven, a symbol of perfection in Tajik culture.
tk: A blue field with a white Southern Cross at the right and a yellow canoe sailing to the left. The canoe stands for the Tokelauan people's voyages and heritage, the Southern Cross is a navigation constellation, and the blue represents the ocean. It was adopted in 2008.
tl: A red field with a black triangle holding a white triangle, and a white star at its centre, and a yellow triangle. Red stands for the struggle for independence, black for the obscurantism to overcome, yellow for the trace of colonialism, and white for peace. The star is the guiding light.
tm: A green field with a vertical red band at the hoist holding five carpet guls and olive branches, and a white crescent and five stars. The carpet patterns stand for the five main tribes and traditional carpet-weaving. The crescent stands for the bright future and Islam, and the olive branches for neutrality.
tn: A red field with a white disc holding a red crescent and star. Red stands for the blood shed against foreign rule. The crescent and star are symbols of Islam and of the sun and the moon. The flag was based on the Ottoman flag and has been in use since 1831.
to: A red field with a white rectangle at the canton holding a red cross. Red stands for the blood of Christ, and the cross for Christianity, as Tonga is a deeply Christian country. White stands for purity. It was adopted in 1875 under King George Tupou I.
tr: A red field with a white crescent and star. Red is said to stand for the blood of the martyrs, and the crescent and star are symbols of Islam and the Ottoman Empire. A legend holds that the crescent and star are the reflection in a pool of blood after a battle.
tt: A red field with a white-edged black diagonal stripe. Red stands for the sun, vitality and the warmth of the people, black for the dedication and strength, and white for the sea and equality. The diagonal stripe symbolises the unity of the people.
tv: A light blue ensign with the Union Jack and nine yellow stars at the fly. The stars represent the nine islands, arranged in the actual geographic layout. Light blue stands for the Pacific Ocean, and the Union Jack for the country's links to the British Commonwealth.
tw: A red field with a blue canton holding a white sun with 12 rays. Red stands for the blood of revolutionaries and fraternity, blue for liberty and justice, and white for equality and honesty. The 12 rays stand for the 12 months and the 12 traditional Chinese hours of the day.
tz: A green and blue diagonal split with a black diagonal band edged in yellow. Green stands for the natural vegetation and agriculture, yellow for mineral wealth, black for the Swahili people, and blue for the Indian Ocean and lakes. It combines the colours of the flags of Tanganyika and Zanzibar.
ua: Blue over yellow horizontal stripes. The colours are said to represent a blue sky over fields of golden wheat. Blue and yellow were also used in the coat of arms of historic Ukrainian lands, and the flag has been a symbol of the nation's identity and independence.
ug: Six horizontal stripes of black, yellow, red, black, yellow and red, with a white disc holding a grey crowned crane. Black stands for the African people, yellow for sunshine and the land's wealth, and red for the brotherhood of the African people. The crane is the national bird, known for its gentle nature.
um: The United States Minor Outlying Islands use the flag of the United States: thirteen red and white stripes with a blue canton of white stars. The stripes represent the original thirteen colonies, and the stars the states.
us: Thirteen red and white horizontal stripes, with a blue canton holding 50 white stars. The stripes represent the original thirteen colonies and the stars the 50 states. Red stands for valour and hardiness, white for purity and innocence, and blue for vigilance, perseverance and justice.
uy: Nine white and blue horizontal stripes with a white canton holding a golden Sun of May. The nine stripes stand for the original nine departments, and the sun with a human face and 16 rays stands for independence. It is inspired by the flag of Argentina and the United States.
uz: Blue, white and green horizontal stripes separated by thin red lines, with a white crescent and twelve stars at the upper hoist. Blue stands for the sky and water, white for peace and purity, green for nature, and red for the vital force. The crescent stands for rebirth and the twelve stars for the months or the zodiac.
va: A square flag split vertically into yellow and white halves, with the crossed keys of St Peter and the papal tiara on the white side. Yellow and white are the colours of the papacy. The golden key stands for spiritual power in heaven, and the silver key for earthly authority.
vc: Blue, yellow and green vertical stripes with three green diamonds in a V shape on the yellow band. Blue stands for the sky and sea, yellow for the sunshine and the warm spirit of the people, and green for the lush vegetation. The diamonds form the letter V for Vincent and the islands' nickname, the 'Gems of the Antilles'.
ve: Yellow, blue and red horizontal stripes with an arc of eight white stars on the blue band. Yellow stands for the land's wealth, blue for the sea, and red for the blood shed for independence. The eight stars stand for the provinces which declared independence from Spain.
vg: A British Blue Ensign with the Union Jack and the territory's coat of arms on the fly. The shield shows Saint Ursula in white with a golden halo, and eleven lamps, from the legend of Saint Ursula and her 11,000 virgins. It stands for purity and the territory's name, 'Virgin Islands'.
vi: A white field with a golden eagle holding an olive branch and arrows, with a shield in the colours of the United States, flanked by the letters V and I. The olive branch stands for peace and the arrows for defence. The eagle represents the United States, and the letters stand for Virgin Islands.
vn: A red field with a large yellow five-pointed star in the centre. Red stands for the revolution and the blood shed for independence, and the yellow star stands for the Communist Party leading the nation. The five points stand for the five main social classes: workers, peasants, intellectuals, youth and soldiers.
vu: A red and green horizontal split with a black triangle edged in yellow and a yellow Y shape, with a boar's tusk and two namele leaves. Red stands for the blood of pigs and men, green for the lush islands, black for the Melanesian people, and yellow for the Christian light. The tusk and leaves symbolise the peace and prosperity of the islands.
wf: A red field with a French tricolour in the canton and a white saltire cross. The French tricolour shows the territory's link to France, and the white saltire cross on red is a traditional design associated with the local kings of the islands.
ws: A red field with a blue canton holding five white stars in the shape of the Southern Cross. Red stands for courage, blue for freedom, and white for purity. The Southern Cross is a constellation seen in the sky above Samoa.
xk: A blue field with a gold map of Kosovo and six white stars in an arc. Blue and gold come from the flag of the European Union, reflecting aspirations to join it. The six stars stand for the six major ethnic groups: Albanians, Serbs, Turks, Roma, Gorani and Bosniaks.
ye: Red, white and black horizontal stripes. The Pan-Arab colours: red stands for the blood of martyrs and the unity of the nation, white for a bright future, and black for the dark past. It was adopted when North and South Yemen unified in 1990.
yt: Mayotte uses the French tricolour of blue, white and red vertical stripes as its official flag. It is an overseas department of France. An unofficial local flag shows a seahorse and the island's emblem on a white background.
za: A flag with a green Y shape that splits into two horizontal bands, with a black triangle and yellow border at the hoist, red above and blue below. It was adopted in 1994 after the end of apartheid. The Y shape stands for the convergence of diverse elements into unity. The colours have no official meaning, though they are often linked to the land, the blood shed and the sky.
zm: A green field with an orange eagle in flight over three vertical stripes of red, black and orange at the fly. Green stands for the country's natural resources and vegetation, red for the struggle for freedom, black for the people, and orange for the mineral wealth, especially copper. The eagle stands for the people's ability to rise above problems.
zw: Seven horizontal stripes of green, yellow, red and black with a white triangle holding a red star and the Zimbabwe bird. Green stands for agriculture, yellow for mineral wealth, red for the blood shed in the struggle for freedom, and black for the African majority. The white triangle stands for peace, the star for the nation's hope, and the soapstone bird for the heritage of Great Zimbabwe.
